analysis:
The change adds only a test file, provider-swift/Tests/DarkbloomCLITests/SandboxWorkDiskTests.swift (433 lines). It adds no production code and changes no runtime behavior, so it adds no attack surface.

The tests exercise a `darkbloom sandbox setup --disk` feature whose implementation (SandboxWorkDisk, SandboxInstaller, SandboxSetupFlow) was not supplied. They encode these behaviors:
- `--disk` paths are normalized to absolute paths.
- Volume checks cover APFS, ownership on, local, writable, and mounted at its own /Volumes/<name>.
- Ownership-off drives get a shell-quoted `sudo diskutil enableOwnership` fix (test line 80-82 confirms single-quote escaping).
- The ownership fix is run only after interactive owner consent, and only with a foreground terminal (lines 149-157).
- Setup refuses when the downloaded installer does not support `--disk`, before running the plan or the install.
- Setup stops before any download when the work disk is not ready.

Relevant boundary: TB-013 / T-061 (installer and add-on run as the Mac's owner) and A-019. The tests suggest sensible guards: user consent before sudo, no command without a terminal, shell-quoting, and a fail-closed unmounted check. Whether the production code actually implements these is outside the supplied evidence.

Questions for integration on the production side, which this PR's visible content cannot answer:
1. How the quoted `fix` string is executed. `runInForeground` should avoid shell interpolation of mount-point names.
2. Whether `--disk` arguments pass to the installer via an argv array, not a shell.
3. Whether an attacker-created /Volumes entry on a candidate list can mislead the user. The tests show candidates are validated by statfs mount-point equality.

The external drive is a possible cache-storage or availability interaction with T-041, but this is a sandbox work disk, not the provider prefix cache. No threat-model regression is identifiable from the test file alone.
